summary.title: Sitagliptin at a glance
points: A DPP-4 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes: keeps the gut's incretin hormones active, raising insulin after meals.
Centrally authorised (Januvia, MSD). On its own only when metformin can't be used; many listed combinations.
HbA1c about −0.7 to −0.8 points vs placebo at 24 weeks; slightly less than metformin head-to-head.
TECOS: no extra heart harm and no extra benefit (HR 0.98).
Watch pancreatitis, hypoglycaemia with sulphonylureas or insulin, allergy, bullous pemphigoid, kidney dosing.

exercises.scenario: A newly diagnosed patient with type 2 diabetes and no contraindications to metformin.

questions.prompt: Can Januvia be her first and only tablet?
questions.explanation: Metformin comes first; sitagliptin alone is slightly less effective.

questions.prompt: Her HbA1c falls by 0.7 points. How should you express that effect?
options: As a number needed to treat
questions.explanation: There's no event rate to turn into a relative reduction.

exercises.scenario: A cardiology partner wants to claim Januvia 'protects the heart'.

questions.prompt: What does TECOS support?
options: No extra harm, no extra benefit
questions.explanation: 11.4% vs 11.6%, HR 0.98; heart-failure hospitalisation 3.1% in both.

questions.prompt: What's the only formal contraindication?
questions.explanation: The others are 'should not be used' situations.

summary.title: How it works
points: GLP-1 and GIP raise insulin after meals; DPP-4 breaks them down within minutes; sitagliptin blocks DPP-4.
More insulin, less glucagon, but only when glucose is normal or high.
Glucose-dependence explains the low hypoglycaemia risk alone; sulphonylureas push insulin regardless.
Bioavailability about 87%; 79% leaves unchanged in urine; half-life about 12.4 hours.
Kidneys set the dose: exposure about 2× at GFR 30–45, 4× below 30. Few interactions.

exercises.scenario: A patient on sitagliptin alone asks whether she can get dangerously low blood sugar.

questions.prompt: What's the explanation?
options: Only if taken with a high-fat meal
questions.explanation: The risk comes when a sulphonylurea or insulin is added.

questions.prompt: Her GFR drops from 70 to 35. What happens to sitagliptin exposure?
options: It rises fourfold, as on dialysis
questions.explanation: About 2× at GFR 30–45; about 4× below 30.

exercises.scenario: A pharmacist checks interactions for a patient on digoxin and ciclosporin.

questions.prompt: What does the SmPC say about digoxin?
options: Halve the digoxin dose from the start
Small rise; monitor if at risk
questions.explanation: A small rise, relevant only for those at risk of digoxin toxicity.

questions.prompt: And ciclosporin?
questions.explanation: Sitagliptin has few meaningful interactions.

summary.title: History
points: First DPP-4 inhibitor: FDA 2006, EU centralised licence March 2007; full EPAR.
Assessors doubted the glipizide comparison: low glipizide dose, non-inferiority not convincingly proven.
Combinations grew from metformin and pioglitazone to sulphonylureas and insulin.
2013 EMA pancreas review: no confirmed increased risk; pancreatitis warning harmonised.
Children 10–17: a negative trial, written into the label. Generics now authorised centrally.

exercises.scenario: A generic company plans to promote sitagliptin as 'as effective as a sulphonylurea'.

questions.prompt: What did the EU assessors conclude about the glipizide trial?
questions.explanation: About 40% of patients took 5 mg glipizide a day or less.

questions.prompt: What's true about generic sitagliptin in the EU?
options: Generics need their own heart-outcome trial
questions.explanation: Sitagliptin SUN and Accord, for example.

exercises.scenario: A paediatric endocrinologist asks about using sitagliptin in a 14-year-old.

questions.prompt: What does the label say?
questions.explanation: −0.2 points (95% CI −0.7 to 0.3) vs placebo.

questions.prompt: What does that show about the EU system?
questions.explanation: The paediatric obligation worked as intended.

summary.title: What it's approved for
points: Adults with type 2 diabetes, always as an adjunct to diet and exercise.
Monotherapy only when metformin can't be used.
Dual: with metformin; a sulphonylurea (if metformin can't be used); pioglitazone.
Triple: with metformin plus a sulphonylurea or pioglitazone; or add-on to insulin.
Not named: SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 RAs; the SGLT2 pairing exists only as Steglujan (ertugliflozin).

exercises.scenario: A patient on the highest tolerated sulphonylurea dose, who can't take metformin, isn't controlled.

questions.prompt: Is sitagliptin + sulphonylurea a licensed dual therapy for him?
options: Yes, since metformin can't be used
Only in triple therapy with metformin added
questions.explanation: Both conditions are met.

questions.prompt: What should the doctor consider for the sulphonylurea dose?
questions.explanation: The combination can push glucose too low.

exercises.scenario: Compare Januvia's EU indication with the US label.

questions.prompt: Which statement is right?
options: Only the EU has a metformin condition
Both have the same metformin condition
questions.explanation: The US also adds that it hasn't been studied in people with past pancreatitis.

questions.prompt: Which partner is NOT named in Januvia's own EU indication?
questions.explanation: Steglujan covers the ertugliflozin pairing.

summary.title: Strengths and products
points: Januvia 25, 50 and 100 mg; no lactose; one EU-wide SmPC; MAH MSD (Haarlem).
Duplicate licences: Xelevia and Tesavel.
Generics authorised centrally on bioequivalence, with biowaivers for lower strengths.
Janumet/Velmetia: 50 mg + metformin 850 or 1,000 mg, twice daily.
Steglujan: 100 mg + ertugliflozin 5 or 15 mg, once daily.

exercises.scenario: A patient on Januvia 100 mg plus metformin 1,000 mg twice daily wants one tablet.

questions.prompt: Which product fits, and how is it taken?
options: Januvia 200 mg once daily with metformin
questions.explanation: Each Janumet tablet holds half the daily sitagliptin dose with a metformin dose.

questions.prompt: Why could a generic's 25 mg and 50 mg strengths skip their own human study?
questions.explanation: Bioequivalence was shown at 100 mg.

exercises.scenario: A BD colleague sees 'Xelevia' and 'Tesavel' in an EMA list.

questions.prompt: What are they?
questions.explanation: Authorised from 2007 and 2008; marketing status not checked in this module.

questions.prompt: Which sitagliptin product contains an SGLT2 inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Ertugliflozin 5 or 15 mg plus sitagliptin 100 mg.

summary.title: How it's taken
points: 100 mg once daily, with or without food; continue diet and exercise.
GFR 45 or above: 100 mg; 30–45: 50 mg; below 30 or dialysis: 25 mg, any time.
With metformin or pioglitazone: no change; with a sulphonylurea or insulin: consider lowering them.
Missed dose: take when remembered, never two in a day.
Not in pregnancy, breastfeeding, or ages 10–17; no adjustment for age alone.

exercises.scenario: A 78-year-old with GFR 38 on metformin needs sitagliptin.

questions.prompt: What dose?
questions.explanation: GFR 30–45 → 50 mg. Age alone needs no change.

questions.prompt: What else must be checked?
questions.explanation: Each partner's kidney limits apply too.

exercises.scenario: A patient on dialysis is starting sitagliptin.

questions.prompt: What dose and timing?
questions.explanation: Dialysis removes only about 13.5% in a 3–4 hour session.

questions.prompt: She also takes insulin. What does the SmPC suggest?
questions.explanation: The combination can cause hypoglycaemia.

summary.title: Reading a clinical trial
points: HbA1c is a surrogate endpoint; outcome trials check what it can't show.
SmPC results are least-squares means, usually placebo-corrected.
Intention-to-treat counts everyone; per-protocol counts adherers. TECOS used per-protocol for non-inferiority.
Non-inferiority margin (TECOS 1.3): the upper CI limit (1.09) must stay below it.
Glycaemic equipoise kept HbA1c similar, isolating the drug's own heart effect.

exercises.scenario: TECOS: HR 0.98, per-protocol CI 0.88–1.09, margin 1.3; superiority p = 0.65.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude?
questions.explanation: Safety question answered; benefit question answered with a no.

questions.prompt: Why did TECOS keep HbA1c similar between arms on purpose?
options: Because HbA1c can't be measured reliably for 3 years
To isolate the drug's own effect
questions.explanation: Glycaemic equipoise: HbA1c differed by only 0.29 points.

exercises.scenario: In the 24-week monotherapy trial, HbA1c fell 0.6 on sitagliptin; the placebo-corrected change was 0.8.

questions.prompt: How can the corrected figure be larger than the raw fall?
options: HbA1c rose a little on placebo
The 200 mg arm was pooled into the figure
questions.explanation: Placebo-corrected = change on drug minus change on placebo.

questions.prompt: Why does the metformin head-to-head use per-protocol figures matter?
questions.explanation: Know who was counted.

summary.title: The pivotal trials
points: Registration: nine HbA1c studies (18–52 weeks, about 6,000 patients).
Study 021 alone: −0.8 vs placebo; 200 mg tested but never authorised.
Study 020 with metformin: −0.7 points; the basis of the most common use.
Study 024 vs glipizide: similar HbA1c, far less hypoglycaemia (4.9% vs 32%), but a low glipizide dose.
TECOS: 14,671 with heart disease, HR 0.98; safety, not benefit; no excess pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer.

exercises.scenario: A partner's slide says: 'Sitagliptin beats sulphonylureas: 85% less hypoglycaemia, weight loss.'

questions.prompt: What's the fair caveat?
questions.explanation: The advantages are real, but the comparator was underdosed.

questions.prompt: Why isn't 200 mg available despite slightly better results in Study 021?
options: 200 mg failed to lower HbA1c more than placebo
questions.explanation: Developed, but never licensed.

exercises.scenario: How do the registration trials and TECOS fit together?

questions.prompt: Which statement is right?
questions.explanation: Read each on its own terms.

questions.prompt: Where does TECOS appear in the EU label?
options: As safety data, not an indication
As a heart-protection indication in section 4.1
questions.explanation: The indications are about glycaemic control only.

summary.title: Combination trials
points: Licences name metformin, sulphonylurea, pioglitazone and insulin; Steglujan covers ertugliflozin.
No licence names dapagliflozin, empagliflozin or a GLP-1 RA; no Januvia SGLT2 line.
Starting with metformin: up to −2.1 points, from a high baseline; not comparable with add-on trials.
Adding ertugliflozin to sitagliptin + metformin: about −0.7 points more (VERTIS SITA2).
With insulin: −0.45 points, less insulin and fewer hypoglycaemia episodes.

exercises.scenario: A doctor wants sitagliptin + empagliflozin + metformin for a patient.

questions.prompt: What do the EU licences offer?
questions.explanation: The licensed SGLT2 pairing is ertugliflozin (Steglujan).

questions.prompt: A partner proposes a sitagliptin + dapagliflozin FDC. What evidence exists?
questions.explanation: Genital and urinary infections were more common, as expected for the class.

exercises.scenario: Three columns: alone, + metformin, + metformin + SGLT2.

questions.prompt: Why can't you say starting both medicines together (−2.1) beats adding one (−0.7)?
options: Because the add-on trial was longer
questions.explanation: The −2.1 came from people starting both at once with a high baseline HbA1c.

questions.prompt: What did adding sitagliptin during insulin intensification show?
options: No effect on HbA1c or on the insulin dose
questions.explanation: Severe hypoglycaemia didn't differ.

summary.title: Heart-attack and stroke outcomes
points: TECOS: every outcome within 0.2 points; none significant. Death HR 1.01; heart failure HR 1.00.
Applies to people with CV disease, HbA1c 6.5–8.0%, eGFR 30 or above.
SAVOR (saxagliptin): heart-failure hospitalisation HR 1.27, significant; EXAMINE (alogliptin) HR 1.19, not significant.
Pooled: RR 1.12 with heterogeneity, driven by SAVOR; maybe saxagliptin-specific or chance.
US label: class heart-failure warning; EU: reports TECOS HR 1.00, no warning.

exercises.scenario: A patient with heart failure needs more glucose lowering. A doctor worries about DPP-4 inhibitors.

questions.prompt: What does the evidence say for sitagliptin specifically?
options: It raised heart-failure admissions, like saxagliptin did
TECOS found no increase in heart-failure hospitalisation (HR 1.00)
questions.explanation: Neutral; ESC 2023 lists it as a heart-safe option.

questions.prompt: Which DPP-4 inhibitor trial showed a significant heart-failure increase?

exercises.scenario: Why do the EU and US Januvia labels differ on heart failure?

questions.prompt: Choose the explanation.
options: TECOS showed harm in the US only
US: class warning; EU: TECOS result
The US label has no heart section
The EU carries the same class heart-failure warning
questions.explanation: Same evidence, two regulatory readings.

questions.prompt: Who does TECOS's reassurance cover least well?
options: eGFR below 30, or very high HbA1c
People with eGFR below 60, who were excluded
questions.explanation: eGFR below 30 was excluded; HbA1c was 6.5–8.0%.

summary.title: Side effects
points: Common: hypoglycaemia (mostly with sulphonylurea or insulin), headache.
Not known: allergy incl. anaphylaxis, pancreatitis, bullous pemphigoid, SJS, arthropathy, kidney effects.
Many combination side effects reflect the partner (nausea with metformin, oedema with pioglitazone).
Pancreatitis: stop if suspected, never restart if confirmed.
Serious allergy mostly in the first 3 months: stop and switch treatment.

exercises.scenario: A patient on sitagliptin plus glimepiride has repeated hypoglycaemia.

questions.prompt: What does the SmPC point to?
options: Stop sitagliptin at once and permanently
Sitagliptin causes it on its own
questions.explanation: The risk comes mainly from the sulphonylurea.

questions.prompt: Another patient has severe abdominal pain spreading to the back.
questions.explanation: Typical presentation of pancreatitis.

exercises.scenario: A patient on sitagliptin + pioglitazone has swollen ankles.

questions.prompt: What's the most likely source?
options: A late allergic reaction to sitagliptin
questions.explanation: Many combination side effects reflect the partner medicine.

questions.prompt: An older patient develops tense blisters on the skin.
questions.explanation: The SmPC says stop if suspected.

summary.title: Who shouldn't take it, and interactions
points: One contraindication: allergy to sitagliptin or an ingredient.
'Should not be used': type 1 diabetes, ketoacidosis, pregnancy, breastfeeding, ages 10–17.
Caution: past pancreatitis, severe liver impairment; dose follows GFR.
Few interactions: ciclosporin +29% (not meaningful), digoxin +11% (monitor).
Gaps: strong CYP3A4 inhibitors in severe kidney disease; OAT3 inhibitors tested only in the lab.

exercises.scenario: A pregnant woman with type 2 diabetes is on sitagliptin.

questions.prompt: What does the SmPC say?
questions.explanation: 'Should not be used' is a strong recommendation, not a formal contraindication.

questions.prompt: Which IS a formal contraindication?
questions.explanation: That's the whole list.

exercises.scenario: A patient with GFR 20 is started on clarithromycin.

questions.prompt: What's the concern?
questions.explanation: An open data gap, not a labelled interaction.

questions.prompt: What's the most important interaction in practice?
questions.explanation: It's about effect, not drug levels.

summary.title: Pharmacovigilance
points: PSUSAs added bullous pemphigoid and arthropathy (2015) and thrombocytopenia (2018).
Thrombocytopenia: 307 reports, but six well-documented cases carried the decision.
2013 pancreas review: no confirmed risk; harmonised pancreatitis wording; cancer uncertainty remains.
RMP (generics): no identified risks; pancreatic cancer as potential risk; pregnancy and breastfeeding missing.
NTTP nitrosamine (2022): a manufacturing impurity, not a side effect.

exercises.scenario: Your sitagliptin generic supplier reports an NTTP impurity above the usual limit.

questions.prompt: What kind of issue is it?
options: A new DPP-4 class safety signal
questions.explanation: The FDA temporarily allowed up to 246.7 ng/day to avoid shortages.

questions.prompt: What was the usual acceptable intake for NTTP?
questions.explanation: Australia later set 100 ng/day, matching EMA and Health Canada.

exercises.scenario: How did 307 reports become one label line?

questions.prompt: What drove the decision?
questions.explanation: Quality of evidence beats quantity.

questions.prompt: What does a positive rechallenge mean?
questions.explanation: Strong evidence of cause.

summary.title: ESC guidelines
points: ESC 2023: SGLT2 inhibitors and/or GLP-1 RAs for heart protection in diabetes with atherosclerotic disease.
SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure; either class considered at 10-year risk ≥10%.
Sitagliptin: a heart-safe option for extra glucose control, including in heart failure.
Saxagliptin and pioglitazone aren't recommended in heart failure.
Label trails practice: Januvia's indication doesn't name SGLT2 partners.

exercises.scenario: A patient with diabetes and coronary disease is on metformin. HbA1c is 7.4%.

questions.prompt: What does ESC 2023 recommend for heart protection?
options: An SGLT2 inhibitor and/or GLP-1 RA
questions.explanation: Heart protection is independent of HbA1c.

questions.prompt: Later he needs more glucose lowering, and has heart failure. Is sitagliptin an option?
options: No, all DPP-4 inhibitors are banned
Yes: it's neutral on heart failure
questions.explanation: Saxagliptin and pioglitazone aren't recommended in heart failure.

exercises.scenario: He's now on metformin + empagliflozin + sitagliptin.

questions.prompt: How does that fit the Januvia label?
options: A gap: the label trails practice
questions.explanation: Each medicine is prescribed under its own licence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best describes sitagliptin's place?
options: A drug to avoid in heart disease
A replacement for metformin in heart disease
questions.explanation: That's the guideline's view.

summary.title: The medicine and its story
points: Glucose-dependent incretin protection: low hypoglycaemia risk alone, more with sulphonylureas.
Kidney-cleared: exposure rises as GFR falls, which drives the dose.
First in class, approved on HbA1c; slightly less effective than metformin.
The label kept honest findings: weak glipizide comparison, negative paediatric trial, pancreas review.

exercises.scenario: An investor asks why sitagliptin isn't first-line despite being first in class.

questions.prompt: What's the best answer?
options: It has no EU licence for use on its own
questions.explanation: EPAR: slightly less effective than metformin.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism fact matters most for safety positioning?
questions.explanation: The contrast with sulphonylureas.

exercises.scenario: Connect history with today's label.

questions.prompt: What came of the 2013 pancreas review?
options: A contraindication in anyone with past pancreatitis
questions.explanation: Pancreatic cancer stays a potential risk in the RMP.

questions.prompt: Why is the dose 25 mg below GFR 30?
questions.explanation: Mechanism explains labelling.

questions.prompt: What did the negative paediatric trial lead to?
questions.explanation: Openly reported, label changed.

summary.title: The label in practice
points: Indication ladder: alone (if no metformin), dual, triple, or with insulin.
Products: Januvia, duplicates, generics, Janumet (twice daily), Steglujan (once daily).
Kidney dosing: 100 / 50 / 25 mg at GFR ≥45 / 30–45 / <30.
Lower the sulphonylurea or insulin dose when adding sitagliptin.

exercises.scenario: A 70-year-old on metformin and insulin, GFR 42, HbA1c not at goal.

questions.prompt: Which sitagliptin use applies?
options: Dual therapy with a sulphonylurea instead
questions.explanation: Stable insulin with or without metformin.

questions.prompt: What dose?
What else should be considered?
options: Stop metformin automatically at this age
questions.explanation: Hypoglycaemia risk and the partner's limits.

exercises.scenario: A pharmacy wants to replace Januvia 100 mg + metformin 1,000 mg twice daily with one product.

questions.prompt: Which product and schedule?
questions.explanation: Total sitagliptin stays 100 mg.

questions.prompt: If GFR falls to 35, is Janumet still suitable?
options: Switch to Steglujan, which has no kidney limit
questions.explanation: Sitagliptin alone would fall to 50 mg daily.

questions.prompt: What does the EU indication say about using sitagliptin alone?
options: Whenever the patient prefers it to metformin
Only if metformin can't be used
questions.explanation: The US has no such condition.

summary.title: The evidence
points: HbA1c effects: about −0.7 to −0.8 points; the glipizide comparison was tilted.
TECOS: non-inferior for heart events and heart failure, no benefit, with glycaemic equipoise.
Combinations: many HbA1c add-on trials; no outcome trial with an SGLT2 inhibitor.
Heart failure: SAVOR's signal is saxagliptin-specific or chance; TECOS HR 1.00.

exercises.scenario: A payer asks: 'Should we prefer sitagliptin to reduce heart events?'

questions.prompt: What's the evidence-based answer?
questions.explanation: Non-inferiority ≠ superiority.

questions.prompt: How should you describe TECOS's 0.2-point difference?
options: A 2% proven reduction in heart events
questions.explanation: Give both forms, and say it wasn't significant.

questions.prompt: What's the per-protocol TECOS CI upper limit compared with the margin?
questions.explanation: Below the margin means not worse.

exercises.scenario: A competitor says 'all DPP-4 inhibitors raise heart failure'.

questions.prompt: What does the evidence show?
questions.explanation: Pooled RR 1.12 with heterogeneity, driven by SAVOR.

questions.prompt: Why can't you compare the trials head-to-head?
options: They were all stopped early for harm
questions.explanation: Each column stands on its own.

questions.prompt: Which combination evidence exists for sitagliptin + SGLT2 inhibitors?
questions.explanation: Ertugliflozin is the only licensed pairing.

summary.title: Safety and guidelines
points: Hypoglycaemia comes from the partner; lower sulphonylurea or insulin doses.
Pancreatitis, allergy and bullous pemphigoid: stop; never restart after confirmed pancreatitis.
Safety reviews added pemphigoid, arthropathy and thrombocytopenia; pancreatic cancer is a potential risk.
ESC 2023: SGLT2/GLP-1 RA for heart protection; sitagliptin for extra glucose control, heart-safe.

exercises.scenario: A 65-year-old with heart failure on metformin and dapagliflozin needs more glucose lowering.

questions.prompt: Which option does ESC 2023 consider heart-safe here?
questions.explanation: Saxagliptin and pioglitazone aren't recommended in heart failure.

questions.prompt: Does Januvia's label name dapagliflozin as a partner?
questions.explanation: The label trails practice here.

questions.prompt: Two months in, she reports blistering skin. What next?
options: Halve the dose and see if it settles
questions.explanation: Added to the label through a 2015 PSUSA.

exercises.scenario: Explain how safety knowledge grows after approval.

questions.prompt: Which route added thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: Applied also to sitagliptin/metformin tablets.

questions.prompt: Which item remains 'to watch' in the EU?
questions.explanation: Plus heart failure, a US-only warning.

questions.prompt: In your own words: what's the difference between 'contraindicated' and 'should not be used', with a sitagliptin example of each?
questions.modelAnswer: A contraindication is an absolute bar — for sitagliptin, only allergy to the medicine or an ingredient. 'Should not be used' is a strong recommendation, usually because data are missing or it doesn't work well enough — for example pregnancy, breastfeeding, type 1 diabetes, or children aged 10–17.

summary.title: Sitagliptin: the whole picture
points: First DPP-4 inhibitor: glucose-dependent, kidney-cleared, few interactions.
Second after metformin; many licensed combinations; SGLT2 only via Steglujan.
HbA1c about −0.7 to −0.8 points; TECOS: heart-safe, not heart-protective.
Hypoglycaemia comes from partners; pancreatitis and allergy rules are strict.
Safety reviews added skin, joint and platelet effects; nitrosamines were a quality issue.
ESC 2023: SGLT2/GLP-1 RA first for the heart; sitagliptin for extra glucose control.

questions.prompt: Which regulatory route do EU sitagliptin generics typically use?
questions.explanation: Sitagliptin SUN and Accord, for example.

questions.prompt: Which quality risk should be in the supplier audit plan?
options: Lactose content above the EU threshold
questions.explanation: A manufacturing issue seen in 2022.

questions.prompt: Which promotional claim is NOT supported?
options: Low hypoglycaemia risk when used on its own
questions.explanation: TECOS showed no benefit.

questions.prompt: What sitagliptin dose?
questions.explanation: GFR below 30.

questions.prompt: What about metformin at GFR 28?
questions.explanation: Each partner's limits apply.

questions.prompt: Is sitagliptin acceptable in her heart failure?
questions.explanation: But note TECOS excluded eGFR below 30, so evidence is thinner for her.
